en: The *jaṅghā* together with its increments should be divided into five parts;
the height of the *ṭikkara*, however, shall consist of three of those parts.
By means of the supporting beams growing together, one should construct there a structure possessing five parts; here, that which possesses three parts is the height of the multi-storied building.
With thighs and calves elevated and well-developed, and with a firm, rounded posterior, she who is tall and possesses a graceful gait would be a woman of excellent form.
With its height increased by the upper stories, it likewise becomes a multi-storied mansion; here, being well-established in height, even its mere sight will be endowed with excellence.

As before, there should be an arrangement within the aggregate (skandha), and the constituent parts (ṭhikkarya) are established; through beauty, the various successive actions and mature tasks are adorned.

Just as before, through the arrangement of the aggregates, here too there is the very same tiered arrangement; the various activities of others should be made beautiful by those who possess knowledge.
In this [second] alternative, the height is desired to be equal to the length;
furthermore, the divisions such as the neck and so forth here are also as before.

The multi-storied building itself is held to be long in one direction and short in this [other] direction; wherever there is a distinction such as the neck and so forth, by that [distinction], it is again here as before.
Thus ends the procedure for the ṭhikkara.
Thus concludes the ritual for the multi-storied palace.
A *vaḍabhī* (pediment) is seen somewhere as a support for a female deity;
it should be fashioned according to instruction, either in the Vārendrī or Drāviḍī style.
Because the deities of the three [realms] reside there, one should examine the roof-ridge; one should act according to the instructions of Bārendra or Dābiḍa.
The *vaḍabhī* is considered to be joined [to the wall] at five or six parts;
the *varaṇḍa* above the *chāṇika* has a height equal to its width.
The pinnacle is held to rest perfectly upon a fifth or a sixth part [of the base]; its height, equal to the portion of its elevation, is situated above the *bārendra*.

The Vaḍabhīya style is characterized by a middle section in the Drāviḍa manner; the Dvikhaṇḍikā has one such section, while the Vārendrī and Gauḍa styles are considered to have a single-sectioned vaḍabhī.
Regarding the body of the central roof-ridge (*rgya phubs*): there are two sections of *Dābiḍaba*. As for the single section of the roof-ridge, it follows the systems of Bārendra and Gauda.
The contractions at the back and the front of these should be made by the wise according to their proportions;
this [structure] should be fashioned with central auspicious bands for the sake of visual beauty.

The apex of the back should be properly gathered; the sides should be fully expanded by the skilled artisan; and the central frame and the panels should be made so that they appear beautiful when viewed.
The Drāviḍī [drum] is like a kettle-drum (bherī), with its middle and upper parts [protruding], elevated on both sides by a *cchivara*,
and beautifully adorned with a jar and a lion.

The circular drum is symmetrical; its center is elevated, and both sides have a high central ridge. With the *dāva* and *dava* [wood] as the half-ridge, it is desired that the vase and lion be exquisitely beautiful.
The architectural style of the Vārendrī pediment (vaḍabhī) is seen in all regions;
however, the Drāviḍī pediment is observed only in Kalādi and similar areas.
The function of the *bālenduvaktra* seal is seen in all regions; the *dāpitāva* seal is seen wherever there are parts and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the great palaces: Meru is the abode of the neck of the Fortune of the Mansion; Bhadra is the celestial chariot; Dvīpa is well-known; Kesari, Haṃsa, Vatsa, Garuḍa, Vedāyata, and Vāḍabha [are the others]. Then, for the houses of kings, there are those with four corners, those with eight corners, and so on, up to the circular and the six-cornered varieties, which are to be understood according to their respective configurations.

Furthermore, regarding other great palaces: on Mount Meru, Mandara, and the summit of Sumeru, as well as on the excellent multi-storied mansions that serve as abodes for travel, and on the dwellings of elephants, lions, swans, their young, garuḍas, and the Vedas—their roofs are described [in the same manner]. On the faces that are twice the size of the face of the Vedas, and likewise on the royal palaces, it is exactly the same.
One should understand that the application to the ornaments likewise proceeds according to the divisions of circularity, six, and four.
Having understood Bhadra, Subhadra, Nandana, and Nalina as the fourth, the three Bhadras as the fifth, Śrīvatsa, Ardha, and that which is joined with the name Akhaṇḍa, and likewise Vardhamāna;
That which is known as Gṛharāja, together with Nandana, is remembered as another type, the Kuṭīra;
the Kumbha, Ardhendu, Mahokṣa, Upūga, Taru, Padmālaya, and Vṛttaka are [other varieties].

Knowing this, he who possesses the three, five, and the half-and-a-quarter *śrīvatsa*—the auspicious, the most auspicious, the joyful, the lotus-like, the excellent, and the one endowed with activity—is the self that possesses growth (*vṛddhimān*). He remembers the royal bliss found in whatever house, as well as other multi-storied mansions.
Upon the vase, from the axle-tree of the moon and the *dra-go* [constellations], there is the very entry of excellence.

These [styles] are composed according to four divisions: first, the *Nāgara*; then the *Lāṭa*, the *Ākṣa*, the *Varāṭaka*, and likewise the one known by the name *Drāviḍa*. Due to the influence of various living beings (*sattva*), foreign lands, and dispositions, there are many [other types] based on minor [elements] that have not been mentioned; however, having understood the rule, one should construct them accordingly. The designation [of each style] should be understood from its specific characteristics. One should not construct [a temple] exceeding one hundred *padas* in size.

These cities, adorned with the fourfold divisions and so forth—such as Lāḍhaka, Pradarśaka, and likewise Devīdāsa—are manifested to sentient beings according to their mental dispositions as either small or great abodes.

Those things not explicitly explained should also be expanded upon through study; those who know the ritual procedures should act accordingly. One should understand the names of the temples according to the distinctions of their architectural bases.
Thus ends the rule concerning the characteristics of mares and other such animals.
"One should not do it over a Chinese site" refers to the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the roof-ridge and so forth. || ||
Either for the purpose of meditation in the abodes of deities, such as single cities and so forth,
or for the purpose of enshrining the Buddhas according to the sequence of the seats of the four Buddhas.
The ultimate meaning of meditative concentration is the single roof over the dwellings of the gods.
Furthermore, for the sake of the abiding of the Buddhas, the seats of the four Buddhas are arranged in successive order.
Or, for the sake of constant enjoyment of desires by yogi-kings,
one should likewise construct houses such as Mānasa and others for the attainment of meditation and other spiritual goals.
The King of Yogins, who constantly teaches abiding or joy, [should...]
The house itself should be made in accordance with the mind and so forth, in order to accomplish meditative concentration and the rest.
A pavilion should be constructed with four archways, or else a *ṭhikkarī* should be made;
in that *ṭhikkarī*, a fourth [archway] should be fashioned, provided with a gateway (*toraṇa*).
One should also construct a multi-storied mansion with four parts arranged like a mandala.
The multi-storied mansion shall consist of small chambers, and it should be constructed together with a gateway arch.
Furthermore, the pillars should be raised from the top of the pavilion by as many parts as they are established from the ground,
or they may be considered slightly less.
The height of the roof over the assembly hall should be equal to the thickness of the wall; it should not be less than that, though others also desire it to be otherwise.
Those portions belonging to the *Ṭhikkaryā* and so forth have already been proclaimed;
they shall be described later, and they are to be performed here in their respective ways.
The portions belonging to the *Khaṅ pa brtsegs ma* (Stacked House) and so forth are well known as before; those that will be mentioned again are to be performed here accordingly.
Above those two, moreover, the neck and the fillet are beautiful with their essential form;
the *caitya* is joined at the *ṭhikkarī*, and at the *maṇḍavī* there is again the *ghaṭa*.
Furthermore, regarding the cloth:
upon those [elements], there is the neck and the beautiful Vimalagarbha; likewise for the tiered pavilion (kūṭāgāra), the desired stūpa, and the assembly hall (upasthānaśālā).
Whether it be a monastery, a hostel, or a hall, or even caves in that very place, the windows and doors must be constructed without crowding; it should not be otherwise.
In a temple, a communal hall, or likewise in any other building, the lattices should be constructed so as not to obstruct one another; it shall not be otherwise than this.
Having extracted the formal figures according to their proper places, one should again arrange them in rows; this is the sequence for the composition of the *karmasaṃgati*.

The form should be established according to its proper state by means of the assistant of the supreme ritual action; then, once again, the house itself [should be prepared]. Such is the sequence of the procedure.
The ritual procedure for the characteristics of the four abodes, the dhyāna-abode, and so forth.
This is the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the four houses, the meditation house, and so forth.
